texts.title: The Lost Dog
texts.body: Maya's dog Biscuit ran out of the gate one morning. Maya searched the whole street calling his name. She checked under the bushes and behind the garage. Her neighbour Mr Peters came out and asked what was wrong. When Maya explained, he pointed toward the park. Maya ran to the park and found Biscuit sitting near the pond, wagging his tail at the ducks. Maya knelt down and hugged him tightly. She clipped his lead on and walked home slowly, making sure the gate was locked behind her. From that day on, Maya always checked the gate twice before letting Biscuit outside. She also wrote her phone number on a tag and attached it to his collar so anyone who found him could call her.

texts.title: Learning to Ride
texts.body: Thabo had been trying to learn to ride his bicycle for three weeks. Every afternoon he tried, and every afternoon he fell. His knees were covered in plasters. His older sister Nomsa watched from the porch. One day she came down and held the back of the seat while Thabo pedalled. 'Don't let go,' Thabo said. 'I'm going to let go now,' Nomsa warned. Before Thabo could protest, she released the seat. He wobbled, steadied himself, and kept going. When he reached the end of the street, he realised he had been riding on his own. He spun the bike around with a huge grin. Nomsa was already jumping up and down. 'You've got it!' she shouted. Thabo rode back up the street without stopping once.

texts.title: The New Student
texts.body: On Monday a new girl named Priya joined Class 4B. She sat in the empty desk next to the window and didn't speak to anyone at break. She ate her lunch alone, reading a book about space. Kofi noticed her sitting by herself and carried his tray over. 'Is space interesting?' he asked, nodding at her book. Priya looked up, surprised. 'Very,' she said. 'There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on Earth.' Kofi sat down. By the time the bell rang they had argued cheerfully about whether Mars would ever have cities, and Priya had laughed twice. The next morning she came in early and saved Kofi a seat. He had not even asked her to.

texts.title: The Argument
texts.body: Samuel and Lena had been best friends since Grade 1. One Tuesday they argued over a ball during break. Samuel said it was his turn. Lena said she had been waiting longer. Neither of them would give in. By the end of school they were not speaking. That evening Samuel thought about it while eating his dinner. He remembered that Lena had shared her crisps with him on Monday when he forgot his snack. He felt a small knot of guilt in his chest. The next morning he arrived early and knocked on Lena's classroom door. 'I'm sorry I was unfair,' he said. Lena was quiet for a moment. 'I was being stubborn too,' she admitted. They walked to break together, and this time they took turns without anyone having to count.

texts.title: Grandma's Chickens
texts.body: Zoe had never been on a farm before. When she arrived at her grandmother's house in the hills, the first thing she heard was the crowing of roosters. Her grandmother showed her the chicken coop, a small wooden building where twelve hens lived. Grandma explained that the hens laid one egg each per day, and that collecting eggs was the morning job. Zoe reached carefully into each nesting box and placed the warm eggs in a basket. One hen pecked at her hand, and she jumped back. 'She's just nervous,' Grandma said calmly. 'Move slowly and she'll get used to you.' By the third day, Zoe could collect all twelve eggs without a single peck. At breakfast she scrambled six of them herself, cracking the shells on the side of the pan the way Grandma had shown her.

texts.title: The School Play
texts.body: Amara had been given the biggest part in the Grade 4 play. She was the narrator, which meant she had thirty-two lines to remember. For two weeks she practised every night. She stood in front of her bedroom mirror and spoke her lines to her reflection. On the morning of the performance, she woke up with a stomach full of butterflies. She could not eat her breakfast. When she walked onto the stage and saw the rows of parents, her mind went completely blank. But then her teacher, standing in the wings, gave her a small nod. Amara took a breath and began. Each line came after the last without a gap. When she finished, the hall filled with applause. Her mother was wiping her eyes in the front row. Amara walked off stage on shaking legs — and then immediately wanted to do it all over again.

texts.title: The Injured Bird
texts.body: One morning Sipho found a small bird sitting on the path near the school gate. It fluttered its wings but could not fly. One wing hung at a wrong angle. Sipho picked it up carefully, feeling its heart beating rapidly against his fingers. He carried it to the science teacher, Mr Dlamini, who wrapped it gently in a cloth and put it in a shoebox with air holes. Mr Dlamini called a local wildlife rescue centre after school. The rescue worker came and said the bird had a sprained wing. 'With rest it should recover,' she said. She left her number on a card so Sipho could check on the bird's progress. Three weeks later the rescue centre sent a message: the bird had been released and was flying. Sipho put the message in his class nature journal.

texts.title: The Savings Jar
texts.body: Liam wanted a new football. The one he wanted cost R150. His mother said she could not buy it right now. 'But I can help you earn it,' she said. She offered him R5 for every day he made his bed and R10 for every time he washed the dishes after dinner. Liam bought a glass jar and put it on his desk where he could see it. Every coin went in. He counted the money each Sunday. By the fifth week the jar held R120. On the sixth Sunday it held R155. He walked with his mother to the sports shop, paid at the counter, and carried the box home himself. The football lasted two full seasons. When he eventually needed a new one, he already knew exactly how to save for it.

texts.title: The Sandcastle Competition
texts.body: On the last day of the holiday, the beach club held a sandcastle competition. Teams had one hour to build the tallest, most detailed castle they could. Nia and her cousin Dev decided to work together even though they had very different ideas. Dev wanted to build high. Nia wanted to carve windows and a drawbridge. They argued for the first five minutes, then Nia suggested a plan: Dev would handle the towers and Nia would decorate the walls. They agreed and started immediately. Dev piled the sand high and packed it firmly. Nia carved windows, a gate, and a moat. When the judge walked past with her clipboard, she paused at their castle for a long time. 'Most creative detail,' the judge announced, handing them a small ribbon. Nia held the ribbon and Dev said it was the best competition he had ever entered.

texts.title: Too Tired to Remember
texts.body: It was the week before exams and Esi was studying until midnight every night. She read the same pages twice because she could not concentrate. Her father noticed the light under her door at 11 o'clock. He knocked and came in. 'Your brain needs sleep to store what you've learnt,' he said. 'Studying late damages your memory, not helps it.' Esi argued that she had too much to cover. Her father sat on the edge of the bed. 'Test me,' he said. 'Tell me three things you just read.' Esi tried, but could only name one. The next night her father set a rule: lights out at 9:30. On the morning of the first exam, Esi ate breakfast, felt calm, and remembered everything she needed. She scored the highest mark she had earned all year.

texts.title: How Butterflies Develop
texts.body: A butterfly's life begins as a tiny egg on a leaf. When the egg hatches, a caterpillar comes out. The caterpillar's only job is to eat. It feeds on leaves constantly and grows much bigger over several weeks. When the caterpillar is fully grown, it forms a hard outer case around itself called a chrysalis. Inside the chrysalis the caterpillar's body changes completely. This process is called metamorphosis. After about two weeks the case splits open and a butterfly crawls out. At first its wings are soft and wet. The butterfly pumps fluid into its wings until they are firm and dry. Then it flies off to find food and, eventually, a partner to lay eggs with. The whole cycle then begins again. Most butterflies live for only two to four weeks as adults, though some species live longer.

texts.title: Why We Should Recycle
texts.body: When we throw away plastic, glass, or paper in the wrong bin, it goes to a landfill — a large hole in the ground where rubbish is buried. Landfills take up space, create pollution, and can harm the soil and nearby water. Recycling solves this by turning used materials into new ones. A single glass bottle can be melted and reshaped into a new bottle using less energy than making one from scratch. Recycled paper saves trees from being cut down. Recycled plastic stops it from reaching rivers and oceans, where it harms fish and birds. Most cities have a recycling system. All you have to do is sort your rubbish into the correct bins. Paper and cardboard go in one bin, glass and metals in another, and food waste in a third. Small actions, done by many people, add up to a very large difference.

texts.title: How Bees Make Honey
texts.body: Honey bees collect a sweet liquid called nectar from flowers. A bee sucks up the nectar through a tube-like tongue and stores it in a special part of its body called the honey stomach. Back at the hive, the bee passes the nectar to a younger bee, which chews it and mixes it with chemicals from its body. This breaks the nectar down into simpler sugars. The bees then spread the processed nectar across the walls of the hive cells. They fan it with their wings to remove the water. When the water content drops low enough, the nectar thickens into honey. The bees seal the cell with wax to store the honey. A single hive can make up to 30 kilograms of honey in a good year. The bees use the honey as food during winter when flowers are not available.

texts.title: The Water Cycle
texts.body: Water moves in a continuous circle around the Earth. This movement is called the water cycle. It begins when the sun heats water in the sea, rivers, and lakes. Some of the water turns from liquid into invisible water vapour, which rises into the air. This process is called evaporation. As the vapour rises, it cools down and turns back into tiny water droplets. The droplets clump together to form clouds. This process is called condensation. When enough droplets gather, they become too heavy to stay in the air and fall back to Earth as rain, snow, or hail. This is called precipitation. The water flows back into rivers and seas or soaks into the ground. From there it evaporates again and the cycle starts over. The water cycle keeps fresh water moving to all parts of the Earth.

texts.title: How Libraries Work
texts.body: A public library is a place where anyone can borrow books and other materials for free. Libraries are run by local governments and paid for by taxes. Every person who lives in the area can get a library card. With a library card you can borrow up to a set number of books at a time, usually between four and ten. You keep them for two or three weeks and then return them. If you want a book the library does not have, a librarian can request it from another branch. Libraries also have computers for public use, quiet study spaces, and regular reading programmes for children. When a book is returned it is checked in, shelved in the correct section, and made available for the next person. Libraries are especially important for people who cannot afford to buy books themselves.

texts.title: Why Sleep Matters
texts.body: Children between the ages of six and twelve need between nine and eleven hours of sleep every night. Sleep is not just rest — it is an active time for the brain. While you sleep, your brain sorts through the events of the day and moves important information from short-term to long-term memory. This is why students who sleep well after studying remember more the next day. Sleep also allows the body to repair itself. Growth hormones are released mainly during deep sleep, which is why children who sleep enough tend to grow properly. A lack of sleep causes difficulty concentrating, irritability, and slower reactions. Over time, regular sleep loss is linked to problems with immune function and mental health. Going to bed at the same time each night helps the body fall into a healthy rhythm.

texts.title: How Earthquakes Happen
texts.body: The Earth is made up of large pieces of rock called tectonic plates. These plates float on a layer of hot, partially melted rock. They move very slowly — only a few centimetres per year — but they are always moving. Where two plates meet is called a fault line. When the plates grind against each other, pressure builds up. Eventually the pressure becomes too great and the plates shift suddenly. This sudden movement sends waves of energy through the ground. These waves are what we feel as an earthquake. The point underground where the earthquake starts is called the focus. The point directly above it on the surface is called the epicentre. Earthquakes near the surface are usually more damaging than deep ones. Scientists called seismologists use instruments called seismographs to detect and measure earthquakes anywhere on Earth.

texts.title: The Postal Service
texts.body: Before telephones and the internet, letters were the main way to send information from one place to another. The postal service collected letters from people, sorted them, and delivered them to the correct address. The earliest organised postal service was in ancient Persia over 2 500 years ago — riders on horses carried messages between cities. In the 1800s railways made postal services much faster. By the 1900s airmail allowed letters to cross continents in days. Today most personal messages are sent digitally, but postal services still carry important documents, parcels, and official letters. Each country has its own postal service, and international agreements allow letters to be delivered almost anywhere in the world. The postal service is one of the oldest human systems for sharing information across long distances.

texts.title: How Plants Make Food
texts.body: Plants make their own food using a process called photosynthesis. This process happens mainly in the leaves, which contain a green substance called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll captures energy from sunlight. The plant uses that energy, together with water from the soil and carbon dioxide from the air, to make sugar. The sugar is the plant's food. Oxygen is released as a waste product during this process — which is why plants produce the oxygen that animals and humans need to breathe. Without sunlight, photosynthesis cannot happen, so plants placed in dark rooms eventually die. Water reaches the leaves through thin tubes inside the stem and roots. Carbon dioxide enters through tiny holes in the leaf surface called stomata. Photosynthesis is one of the most important chemical processes on Earth because it is the starting point of almost all food chains.

texts.title: Why Washing Hands Works
texts.body: Germs are tiny organisms that cannot be seen without a microscope. Some germs cause illness when they enter the body. They spread easily from surfaces to hands to face — particularly when people touch their mouth, nose, or eyes. Washing hands with soap removes germs from the skin. Soap works by breaking down the outer layer of a germ so that it can be washed away with water. Plain water alone removes some germs but not as many as soap does. To wash effectively, you should rub all surfaces of both hands for at least 20 seconds — roughly the time it takes to hum the Happy Birthday song twice. Key times to wash are before eating, after using the toilet, after coughing or sneezing, and after touching animals. Regular handwashing is one of the simplest and most effective ways to prevent the spread of illness.

items.title: The Seasons
items.passage: Seasons change because the Earth moves around the sun at a slight angle. When one part of the Earth tilts toward the sun, it receives more heat and light — this is summer. When that same part tilts away, it receives less heat — this is winter. Spring and autumn come between these two extremes. In many parts of the world, four seasons occur each year. Near the equator, however, there are only two seasons: a wet season and a dry one. The length of each season varies depending on where in the world you live. Countries near the poles experience nearly continuous night during winter and nearly continuous daylight during summer.

items.title: Making Bread
items.passage: Bread is one of the oldest foods in the world. To make basic bread you need flour, water, yeast, and salt. Yeast is a tiny living organism. When it is mixed with warm water and flour, it feeds on the sugars in the flour and produces gas. This gas makes the dough rise. The dough must rest in a warm place for at least one hour so the yeast can work. Then it is shaped and baked in a hot oven. The heat kills the yeast and sets the shape of the bread. The outside browns and hardens while the inside stays soft. Different countries add different ingredients to create their own traditional varieties.

items.title: Desert Animals
items.passage: Deserts are some of the harshest places on Earth. Very little rain falls and temperatures can reach extreme highs during the day. Despite this, many animals have adapted to survive there. The camel stores fat in its hump, which provides energy when food is scarce. Its wide, flat feet prevent it from sinking into loose sand. Many desert animals, such as lizards and scorpions, are nocturnal — they rest underground during the hottest part of the day and come out at night when it is cooler. Some small desert mammals get all the water they need from the food they eat, never drinking at all. These remarkable adaptations allow animals to thrive in a place most creatures could not survive.

items.title: The Ocean
items.passage: Oceans cover more than 70 per cent of the Earth's surface. They are home to the largest variety of life on the planet. The ocean can be divided into several zones based on how deep and dark the water is. Near the surface, sunlight reaches the water and plants can grow — this is called the sunlit zone. Below this, very little light penetrates. Animals in these darker zones have adapted to live without sunlight, and many produce their own light through a process called bioluminescence. The ocean also plays a key role in regulating the Earth's climate by absorbing heat from the sun and distributing it around the planet. Without the ocean, surface temperatures would be far more extreme.

items.title: City Water Systems
items.passage: The water that comes out of a tap has made a long journey before it reaches your home. It usually starts as rainwater collected in a reservoir — a large, specially built lake. From the reservoir, the water travels through underground pipes to a treatment plant. At the treatment plant, the water is cleaned using several processes. Sand and gravel filters remove dirt and particles. Chemicals called chlorine are added to kill harmful bacteria. The treated water is then pumped through a network of pipes beneath streets and buildings to reach homes and schools. Engineers monitor the system constantly to ensure water quality and pressure. Without this system, getting clean water to millions of people in a city would be impossible.

items.title: Migration
items.passage: Every year, billions of animals travel long distances to find food, warmer weather, or safe places to raise their young. This behaviour is called migration. Birds are perhaps the best-known migrants. The Arctic tern travels from the Arctic to Antarctica and back each year — a journey of about 70 000 kilometres. Wildebeest in East Africa follow the rains across the Serengeti in enormous herds. Even some fish migrate. Salmon are born in freshwater rivers, swim to the ocean as adults, and return to the same river where they hatched to lay their eggs. Scientists are still studying how animals navigate such vast distances, using the stars, the sun, and even the Earth's magnetic field.

items.title: Forests
items.passage: Forests cover about 31 per cent of the Earth's land surface. They are home to more than 80 per cent of all land-based animal and plant species. Forests produce oxygen, filter water, and hold soil in place to prevent erosion. They also absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which helps to slow climate change. Tropical rainforests, found near the equator, are the most diverse. A single hectare of rainforest can contain over 400 species of trees. Temperate forests, found in cooler regions, lose their leaves in autumn and grow them back in spring — these are called deciduous forests. Despite their importance, forests are shrinking worldwide due to logging, farming, and land clearing.

items.title: Ancient Libraries
items.passage: Before the internet, a library was the most important place a person could go to find information. The ancient library of Alexandria in Egypt was one of the largest in the world, holding hundreds of thousands of scrolls. Today most public libraries contain both physical books and digital collections. Libraries are organised using a classification system. In most English-speaking countries, the Dewey Decimal System is used. Each book is given a number based on its subject, making it easy to find on the shelves. Librarians help people locate information and suggest books based on the reader's interests. Many libraries also run programmes to help adults who struggle with reading improve their skills. Libraries remain one of the most powerful tools for learning available to everyone.

items.title: The Human Heart
items.passage: The heart is a muscle about the size of a fist. It pumps blood around the body constantly, every second of your life, without ever stopping to rest. The heart has four sections, called chambers. The right side receives blood from the body and sends it to the lungs to pick up oxygen. The left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pumps it out to the rest of the body. Each heartbeat makes the heart contract and then relax. At rest, a healthy heart beats between 60 and 100 times per minute. During exercise it beats faster to deliver more oxygen to working muscles. You can feel this if you press two fingers gently against your wrist or the side of your neck.

items.title: Weather Forecasting
items.passage: A weather forecast tells you what the weather is likely to be in the coming hours or days. Meteorologists are scientists who study the atmosphere and use data from satellites, weather stations, and balloons to predict weather. They look at temperature, air pressure, wind direction, and humidity. When warm, moist air meets cold air, rain often follows. High air pressure usually brings settled, dry conditions. Low pressure brings clouds and rain. Modern computers can process enormous amounts of weather data very quickly, which makes forecasts more accurate than they used to be. Most forecasts are reliable for about five to seven days. Beyond that, the atmosphere becomes too complex to predict with confidence. Even with the best tools, weather can still surprise us.

items.title: Dinosaurs
items.passage: Dinosaurs lived on Earth for about 165 million years before disappearing around 66 million years ago. They came in an enormous range of sizes. Some were smaller than a chicken. Others, like the Argentinosaurus, may have been over 30 metres long and weighed as much as 80 tonnes. Dinosaurs were reptiles, but they were not cold-blooded in the same way as modern lizards. Evidence suggests many were warm-blooded and some were covered in feathers. Birds are the living descendants of a group of dinosaurs called theropods. The most widely accepted explanation for the extinction of non-bird dinosaurs is that a large asteroid struck the Earth, blocking sunlight and causing rapid climate change.

items.title: The Solar System
items.passage: Our solar system consists of the sun and everything that orbits it. There are eight planets in the solar system. The four closest to the sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars — are small and rocky. The four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune — are much larger and made mostly of gas or ice. Earth is the third planet from the sun and the only one known to support life. The sun makes up about 99.8 per cent of all the mass in the solar system. It produces energy through a process called nuclear fusion. The solar system also contains moons, asteroids, comets, and dwarf planets such as Pluto. It takes Earth 365 days to complete one orbit around the sun.

items.title: Ancient Egypt
items.passage: Ancient Egypt was one of the earliest civilisations in the world, lasting for over 3 000 years. It developed along the banks of the Nile River, which flooded every year and left behind fertile soil for farming. The Egyptians built enormous stone monuments called pyramids as tombs for their rulers, known as pharaohs. The Great Pyramid of Giza is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and is still standing today. The ancient Egyptians developed one of the earliest writing systems, using picture symbols called hieroglyphics. They also made advances in medicine, mathematics, and astronomy. Much of what we know comes from written records and paintings preserved inside tombs and temples.

items.title: The Rainforest
items.passage: Tropical rainforests grow in warm, wet regions close to the equator. They receive more than 2 000 millimetres of rain per year and are warm throughout all seasons. Rainforests are the most biologically diverse places on Earth. More than half of the world's plant and animal species live there, even though rainforests cover only about 6 per cent of the land surface. The Amazon Rainforest in South America is the largest in the world, covering about 5.5 million square kilometres. Rainforest trees grow very tall to reach sunlight. Their thick canopy of leaves blocks most sunlight from reaching the forest floor. Below the canopy, smaller plants and animals have adapted to living in the dim, sheltered world beneath.

items.title: How Glass is Made
items.passage: Glass is made from sand. At very high temperatures, sand melts and becomes a thick, flowing liquid. To make window glass, the melted sand is mixed with chemicals that lower the temperature needed to melt it and make the glass stronger. The mixture is poured onto a perfectly flat surface of liquid tin. Because it floats on the tin, the glass spreads out into a flat, smooth sheet. It is then cooled slowly in a controlled way so that it does not crack. This cooling process is called annealing. If glass is cooled too quickly it becomes brittle and breaks easily. Coloured glass is made by adding small amounts of metal compounds to the melted sand. The same basic process has been used for hundreds of years.

items.title: How to Plant a Seed
items.procedureText: Planting a seed is simple and gives a plant the best start. First, choose a pot or a patch of soil in a sunny spot. Fill the container with loose, slightly damp soil. Push the seed gently into the soil -- most small seeds need to be planted about twice as deep as they are wide. Cover the seed lightly with soil and press it down gently. Water the soil carefully without using too much water. Label the pot or spot with the plant name and the planting date. Place the pot in a warm, sunny location. Check the soil every day and water when it starts to dry out. Be patient -- seeds can take days to weeks to sprout.

order: Choose a sunny spot and fill with damp soil.
Push seed to correct depth.
Cover lightly and press down.
Water carefully.
Label the pot.
Place in sunny spot.
Check daily; water when dry.

items.title: How to Make a Fruit Salad
items.procedureText: You will need assorted fresh fruit, a knife, a chopping board, a large bowl, and lemon juice. First, wash all the fruit under clean running water. Peel any fruit that needs to be peeled, such as oranges or bananas. Use the knife carefully on the chopping board to cut all fruit into bite-sized pieces. Place the cut fruit into the bowl. Squeeze a small amount of lemon juice over the fruit -- this prevents it from browning. Toss the fruit gently to mix. Taste a piece and add a small amount of honey if you prefer it sweeter. Serve immediately or refrigerate for up to two hours.

order: Wash fruit.
Peel where needed.
Cut into pieces.
Place in bowl.
Add lemon juice.
Toss and taste.
Add honey if desired.
Serve or refrigerate.

items.title: How to Look Up a Word in a Dictionary
items.procedureText: A dictionary lists words in alphabetical order. To find a word, start by identifying its first letter. Turn to the section of the dictionary where that letter starts. Then use the second letter of the word to narrow down the pages. Use the guide words at the top of each page -- these show the first and last word on that page. When you find your word, read the entry carefully. It will show the part of speech (noun, verb, adjective), one or more definitions, and sometimes an example sentence. If your word has more than one meaning, read all the definitions and choose the one that fits your context.

order: Identify the first letter.
Turn to that letter's section.
Use the second letter to narrow pages.
Check guide words at top of page.
Locate the word.
Read the entry -- part of speech, definition(s), example.

items.title: How to Make a Paper Aeroplane
items.procedureText: Start with a rectangular piece of A4 paper. Place it portrait (tall) on a flat surface. Fold the paper in half from top to bottom and then unfold it -- this gives you a centre crease. Fold the top two corners down to meet the centre crease. You should now have a pointed top. Fold the two sides in again toward the centre crease so the pointed tip stays sharp. Fold the whole plane in half along the original centre crease so the folds are on the inside. Fold each wing down so it is flat and parallel to the body. Hold the bottom of the plane and throw it smoothly forward with a slight upward angle.

order: Lay paper portrait.
Fold in half and unfold (centre crease).
Fold top corners to centre.
Fold sides to centre again.
Fold plane in half (folds inside).
Fold each wing flat.
Throw at a slight upward angle.

items.title: How to Care for a Potted Plant
items.procedureText: Caring for a potted plant requires attention to four main things: light, water, soil, and space. First, place your plant in a spot that receives the right amount of light -- check the care label that comes with the plant. Water the plant regularly but do not over-water. Push your finger into the soil -- if the top 2 cm is dry, it is time to water. Pour water slowly until it drains from the bottom holes. Empty the tray underneath after 30 minutes so roots do not sit in water. Once a month, add a small amount of liquid fertiliser to the water. Check every few months whether the plant has outgrown its pot. If roots are coming out of the bottom holes, repot the plant into a slightly larger container.

order: Place in correct light.
Check soil moisture before watering.
Water until drainage.
Empty tray after 30 min.
Add fertiliser monthly.
Check for outgrown pot; repot when needed.

items.title: How to Borrow a Library Book
items.procedureText: To borrow a book from a public library, you will need a valid library card. First, find the book you want using the catalogue -- this can be a computer terminal or a shelf search. Note the book's call number. Use the call number and shelf signs to locate the book on the shelves. Take the book to the issue desk or use the self-service machine. Place your library card on the scanner and follow the prompts, or hand the book to the librarian. A due date will be printed on a slip inside the book or sent to your email. Return the book by the due date to avoid a fine. If you need more time, renew the book online, by phone, or in person before the due date.

order: Get library card.
Search catalogue for book.
Note call number.
Find book on shelves.
Issue at desk or self-service.
Note due date.
Return or renew by due date.

items.title: How to Pack a School Bag the Night Before
items.procedureText: Packing your school bag the night before saves time in the morning and means you are less likely to forget things. Start by checking your timetable to see which subjects you have the next day. Collect all the books, files, and stationery you need for each subject. Check that all homework is complete and packed. Add any permission slips or notes for your teacher. Pack your lunchbox and water bottle. Make sure your PE kit is included if you have sport. Zip the bag closed and place it near the front door or in a set spot so you can grab it quickly in the morning. Do a final check against the timetable.

order: Check timetable.
Collect books and stationery per subject.
Pack completed homework.
Add notes/permission slips.
Add lunchbox and water bottle.
Add PE kit if needed.
Zip and place at door.
Final check against timetable.

items.title: How to Make a Simple Sandwich
items.procedureText: Making a sandwich takes only a few minutes. You will need two slices of bread, a filling of your choice, a spreading knife, and a chopping board. Place both slices of bread on the board. If you are using a spread such as butter or mayonnaise, use the knife to spread it evenly on one side of each slice. Add your filling -- sliced tomato, cheese, egg, or whatever you like -- on top of one slice. Place the second slice on top, spread side down. Press gently so the layers stick together. Use the knife to cut the sandwich in half diagonally or straight across. Serve immediately or wrap in foil or cling wrap for later.

order: Place bread on board.
Spread butter/mayo on one side of each slice.
Add filling to one slice.
Place second slice on top (spread-side down).
Press gently.
Cut in half.
Serve or wrap.

items.title: How to Clean a Paintbrush
items.procedureText: Clean paintbrushes last longer and give better results. After using a brush with water-based paint, hold the brush under running water and rinse it until the water runs clear. Work the bristles gently with your fingers to release all the trapped paint near the base of the bristles. Do not let paint dry at the base as this causes the bristles to splay out. Add a small amount of liquid soap to the bristles and work it in gently with your fingers. Rinse again until the water is completely clear and no soap remains. Gently squeeze out any excess water -- do not wring the bristles. Reshape the bristles with your fingers. Lay the brush flat to dry or hang it with the bristles pointing down.

order: Rinse under running water until clear.
Work fingers near base to release paint.
Add soap; work in gently.
Rinse until water is clear.
Squeeze out water (don't wring).
Reshape bristles.
Lay flat or hang to dry.

items.title: How to Give Directions
items.procedureText: Giving clear directions helps someone get to their destination without getting lost. Start from a landmark both of you know, such as the school entrance. State the direction clearly using left, right, straight on, or compass points if both people understand them. Name the streets or landmarks the person will pass: 'Go past the post office, then turn left at the traffic lights.' Give distances in helpful terms such as 'about 200 metres' or 'about a five-minute walk.' State when the person has arrived: 'You will see a red gate -- that's the entrance.' If there is a tricky point, warn them in advance. Offer to repeat or write the directions down if the route is long or complicated.

order: Start from shared landmark.
State direction (left/right/straight).
Name streets and landmarks to pass.
Give distances in practical terms.
Describe arrival point.
Warn about tricky turns.
Offer to repeat or write down.

items.title: How to Set Up a Simple Absorption Experiment
items.procedureText: This experiment tests which surface absorbs water the fastest. You will need: four different materials (paper, cloth, plastic wrap, and a sponge), an eyedropper, water, and a stopwatch. Lay each material flat on a table. Draw a results table in your notebook with four columns: Material, Drops Used, Time, and Absorbed (Yes/No). Fill the eyedropper with water. Hold it 1 cm above the first material and release exactly three drops. Start the stopwatch immediately. Observe and record whether the water is absorbed or sits on the surface. Record the time for full absorption or note 'not absorbed' after 60 seconds. Repeat for each material. Compare your results and write a conclusion.

order: Lay all materials flat.
Draw results table.
Fill eyedropper.
Release 3 drops from 1 cm height.
Start stopwatch.
Observe and record.
Repeat for all materials.
Compare and write conclusion.

items.title: How to Make a Recycled Paper Collage
items.procedureText: A collage is a picture made by sticking pieces of different materials onto a backing sheet. You will need: old magazines or newspapers, a large sheet of paper or card, scissors, glue, and a pencil. First, lightly sketch your design in pencil on the backing sheet -- this will guide where you place each piece. Browse through the magazines and cut out shapes, colours, and patterns that match your design. Arrange the pieces on the backing sheet before gluing to see how they look. When you are happy with the arrangement, glue each piece down firmly, starting with the largest pieces first. Allow the glue to dry flat. Once dry, add any final details with a pen or marker.

order: Sketch design in pencil on backing sheet.
Cut shapes from magazines.
Arrange pieces (before gluing).
Glue largest pieces first, then smaller.
Allow to dry flat.
Add final details.

items.title: How to Write a Friendly Letter
items.procedureText: A friendly letter has five standard parts. Start with your address and the date in the top right corner. Below that, on the left, write a greeting: 'Dear [Name],' -- include a comma after the name. Write the body of your letter in paragraphs. In the first paragraph, say why you are writing. In the middle paragraphs, share your news or ask your questions. In the final paragraph, round off naturally -- for example, 'I hope to hear from you soon.' End with a closing phrase such as 'Yours sincerely,' or 'With love,' followed by a comma. Sign your name below the closing phrase. If you are posting the letter, fold it into thirds, place it in an envelope, and write the recipient's address on the front and your return address on the back.

order: Write address and date (top right).
Write greeting with comma.
First paragraph: reason for writing.
Middle paragraphs: news/questions.
Final paragraph: close naturally.
Closing phrase + comma.
Sign name.
Fold, envelope, address.

items.title: How to Find a Word's Meaning from Context
items.procedureText: When you come across an unfamiliar word, you can often work out its meaning without a dictionary. First, read the whole sentence carefully -- do not stop at the unknown word. Look at the words directly before and after the unknown word. Ask yourself: is the word describing something, naming something, or telling you what happened? Look for clues in nearby sentences -- sometimes a writer explains a difficult word shortly after using it. Think about the topic of the paragraph and what would make sense there. Substitute a word you know and check whether the sentence still makes sense. If you can do this successfully, you have found the meaning. Check your guess against a dictionary afterwards if you are unsure.

order: Read the whole sentence.
Look at words before and after the unknown word.
Identify the word's function (describe/name/action).
Check nearby sentences for explanation.
Consider the topic and what makes sense.
Substitute a known word and test.
Verify in dictionary if unsure.

items.title: How to Prepare for a Class Presentation
items.procedureText: Giving a good presentation takes preparation. Start by making sure you understand your topic clearly. Write key points on index cards -- one idea per card. Do not write full sentences; use short phrases that will remind you of what to say. Arrange the cards in the order you plan to speak. Practise out loud at least three times -- once alone, once in front of a mirror, and once in front of a family member or friend. Time yourself to make sure you stay within any given limits. On the day, speak slowly and clearly, look up at the audience as often as you can, and hold your cards at chest height. If you lose your place, pause, check your card calmly, and continue.

order: Understand the topic.
Write key points on index cards (short phrases).
Order the cards.
Practise aloud (alone, mirror, audience).
Time yourself.
On the day: speak slowly, look up, hold cards at chest.
If lost: pause, check card, continue.
